newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka NDB float may boost share price.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka NDB float may boost share price.

text.p: The Sri Lankan government's conversion of its National Development Bank (NDB) debentures into ordinary shares is likely to give NDB's share price a boost, analysts said on Wednesday.

NDB said on Wednesday it would convert 27.5 million convertible debentures held by the government into 18.33 million ordinary shares, increasing the bank's issued capital to 35.83 million 10-rupee ordinary shares, from 17.5 million.
The shares will be offered on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in the largest-ever single flotation in Sri Lanka.

Namal Kamalgoda of CTC Eagle Fund Management said the share price was expected to rise because although earnings per share would be diluted by the creation of 18.33 million new shares, fund managers had already factored the expected creation of 27.5 million new shares into the current price.
The convertible debentures were created in 1993 and expected to mature in three tranches starting in 1999.
The company statement said the dilution was reduced in line with the early conversion agreement with the government.
"It will take away the uncertainty associated with the conversion, which lingered over NDB shares," Kamalgoda said.
Analysts said the conversion price would be crucial.
The shares would probably be floated at around 250 rupees ($4.25) each, brokers said. NDB closed on the CSE on Wednesday at 290.25 rupees, after rising to an intra-day high of 295.

"If the debentures are, for example, converted at a discount to the market at about 250 rupees a share, maybe a big investor will be tempted to sell a portion, creating excess supply," said Nanda Nair, head of research at John Keells Stock Brokers.

The float would also substantially enrich government coffers, said an official from the Public Enterprise Reform Commission, which oversees privatisations. "We expect net revenue to the government of between four and five billion rupees," said the official who declined to be identified.
Nair said: "It will also improve NDB share liquidity and make the scrip less volatile."
The new shares will be sold through domestic and foreign offerings, a statement from the bank said on Wednesday.
"As the domestic market is unable to absorb such a large issue, it will be marketed overseas through a "book building" process to achieve the optimum market price for the share," the statement said.
The international marketing programme would target leading international fund managers in New York, London, Edinburgh, Hong Kong and Singapore.
NDB will be assisted by Jardine Fleming and Lehman Brothers, who will be the lead managers to the issue.
The statement said the worldwide marketing campaign would help broaden the bank's ownership base.
This was in line with the NDB's act of incorporation, which does not allow anyone other than the government to hold move than 15 percent of the company, the statement said.

To ensure that the share price was not adversely affected after the flotation, the government and Central Bank, which currently hold 15 and 10 percent of NDB's shares, respectively, had agreed not to sell their existing holdings for at least 18 months, the statement said. ($1 = 58.8 rupees)
